newsitem.title: CHILE: No immediate rate cut--Chile Central Bank chief.
newsitem.headline: No immediate rate cut--Chile Central Bank chief.

text.p: Chilean Central Bank President Carlos Massad said Tuesday he saw no immediate cut in interest rates but that some kind of relaxation of monetary policy was possible later.
Massad, throwing cold water on speculation about an imminent rate cut, told reporters there would be no abrupt end to the Central Bank's tight-credit policy known as "the ajuste," or the adjustment.
"We're at the point where the Central Bank can modify (its monetary policy), in the sense of relaxing the adjustment, but we don't see this as immediate," he said.
"I wouldn't expect any brusque movements. This economy is not managed by fits and starts," he said.
Massad spoke as Chilean stocks leveled off from a dizzying two-day rally in which the blue chip IPSA climbed more than six points, partly on rumors of a rate cut.
The IPSA seesawed through the morning and stood about where it started at 105.74 at 1120 local time.
The Central Bank will continue to exercise a cautious monetary policy with the aim of ensuring official inflation targets, but avoiding a negative impact on economic growth, said Massad.
He attributed the bolsa's rally to the Finance Ministry's announcement of cuts in the 1996 budget late last week.

Consumer prices rose 6.6 percent in Chile last year, just a hair over the government's target of 6.5 percent but close enough for officials to declare the goal met and for the market to speculate about a rate cut.
Massad has said the bank is determined to bring inflation down to levels comparable to those in developed countries -- four percent or so -- by the end of the decade.
